text: Catalog Automation taught you how to chain approval actions in Flow Designer, one stage approving before the next even starts. Change approval workflows are built with that exact same tool and pattern, just triggered on change_request instead of a catalog request.

A common real pattern for Normal changes is two stages. Every Normal change first requires manager approval, regardless of risk. Then the flow checks the calculated risk field from Lesson 11: Low risk moves straight toward Scheduled, while Medium or High risk adds a second stage, CAB approval, chained sequentially after the first.

The branching logic lives inside the flow itself, as a condition evaluated right after manager approval resolves. An If action checks change_request.risk — Medium or High continues into the CAB-approval stage, Low skips straight to moving the change toward Scheduled. This is the real mechanism behind higher risk requiring more approval, not a policy someone has to remember to apply.

While any stage is active, the change record's approval field shows an approval outstanding, and the change itself typically sits pending rather than moving toward implementation. If a manager or CAB rejects at any stage, the flow should route the record back for rework or mark it rejected outright — never leave it silently stalled with no defined next step.

Lesson 10 set up the three change types, Lesson 11 built the risk value, and this lesson is where those two pieces connect into a real working path from created to authorized. What's still missing is what the CAB approval stage actually represents as a real recurring body, not just a step in a flow diagram.

A real branch, evaluated automatically, every time — that's what makes risk-driven approval work in practice. Next up: Change Advisory Board configuration, including the Change Calendar and Conflict Detection that support it.
